title: The last glacial cycle in western Norway—extensive MIS 5d glaciation, multiple glacial advances and LGM glacial advance phases
abstract: We have investigated fine‐grained marine sediments buried under delta sediments and multiple till beds in a tributary valley in western Norway. The marine bed contains bivalves, foraminifera and terrestrial plant material. The fauna and flora are rather poor, but the presence of molluscan species Mytilus edulis and Arctica islandica suggests that Atlantic waters reached the coastal areas at the time of deposition. The age range of radiocarbon dates from about 25 to 50 ka BP conflicts with previous studies from the area and is considered as minimum ages only. This conclusion is supported by amino acid epimerization values in molluscs from the radiocarbon‐dated unit, indicating that it should be correlated with an Early Weichselian, MIS 5c interstadial. The marine unit and overlying delta succession are situated on the outer coast up to 56 m above present sea level, suggesting that they were deposited during a high sea‐level stand following retreat of an extensive MIS 5d glaciation. A compiled Weichselian glaciation curve shows five major glacial advances extending to the outermost coast or beyond. These advances seem to correspond to periods with North Atlantic sea surface cooling. Three till units on top of the delta are interpreted to represent glacier advance prior to the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and during the subsequent deglaciation. Clast fabrics in the lower till and orientation of clastic dikes show an upvalley component opposite to LGM maximum ice‐flow direction. This indicates that initial glacier advance was by fjord glaciers extending to the outer coast while there was limited glacier extent in coastal mountain areas. This interpretation favours fast ice flow along the fjords and major supply of ice from interior mountain areas. Glacier growth in coastal mountains led to merging with fjord glaciers, reorientation of the ice‐flow direction and ultimately maximum glacier extent. Empirical data on ice‐sheet growth are extremely rare and may have been overlooked in many stratigraphic records. Such data are vital for understanding behaviour of ice sheets and in a wider sense, the climate system.

title: Reversible Atlantic overturning despite continued Greenland ice sheet melt
abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is considered vulnerable to irreversible weakening or collapse under global warming and related Greenland ice sheet (GrIS) melt, yet its resilience to either forcing remains poorly constrained. Here, we use a carbon dioxide emission-driven Earth system model with an interactive GrIS to assess AMOC reversibility under a range of idealized carbon dioxide emission pathways that produce near-linear global warming up to 10 kelvins (K), stabilization across 1.5 to 9 K, and subsequent cooling. We find that although the AMOC reaches threshold-defined collapsed states, these do not represent dynamical tipping in this model: The overturning weakens quasi-linearly with global mean temperature increase yet consistently and promptly recovers under cooling. In contrast, GrIS mass loss accelerates with warming, continues through stabilizations, and is only slowed by cooling, committing the planet to long-term sea level rise. These results reveal contrasting resilience across climate system components: Under transient carbon dioxide forcing, AMOC strength remains dynamically reversible despite continued Greenland meltwater input, whereas the GrIS is locked into persistent decline. Our findings underscore the urgency of rapid emission cuts to limit climate overshoot, AMOC weakening, and irreversible ice sheet loss.

title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

title: An Arctic ice shelf in the Last Glacial Maximum rivalled Antarctica’s modern ice shelves
abstract: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02127-6 Ice shelves stabilize marine-terminating ice sheets, and their loss can trigger rapid, irreversible ice-sheet retreat. New geomorphic evidence for a multi-kilometre-thick ice shelf in Baffin Bay during the last glacial period constrains the maximum extents of three surrounding ice sheets and demonstrates that their stability was fundamentally linked.

title: Holocene millennial climate variability influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: A prominent unstable feature, millennial-scale climate oscillation (MCO), punctuated the Holocene. Solar activity and deep ocean variability are generally regarded as the origin of the MCO, yet the dynamics remain debated. Using a Holocene transient simulation with the EC-Earth climate model (8 to 0 ka BP), together with a global compilation of 304 temperature reconstructions, here we identify a robust ~1,350-y oscillatory mode that characterizes Holocene climate variability and is self-sustained and crucially influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions. Within each cycle, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) strengthening evolves with the developing warming and an El Niño-like tropical sea surface temperature (SST) response, accompanied by anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Northward cold advection of the associated enhanced westerly winds off the Antarctic coast overcomes the effect of sea ice retreat to promote AABW formation, ocean stratification, and warming. Positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo, tropical air–sea interaction, and SST-AABW magnify surface warming till AABW reaches its peak. Thereafter, reduced brine rejection from sea-ice retreat weakens AABW, counteracts the warming, and commences a switch to its cooling phase. The dominant periodicity, consistent with that inferred from proxy reconstructions, is confirmed by complementary climate simulations. These results provide an alternative physical mechanism for Holocene millennial-scale climate variability. Under future anthropogenic warming, a positive phase of the oscillation may heighten the positive feedbacks, thereby increasing the risk of rapid climate transformation.

title: Isolated Northern Hemisphere Cooling in an Idealized Model Promotes Ocean Carbon Storage and Glacial-like Ocean Features
abstract: Abstract Earth’s past glacial cycles are paced by orbital insolation changes, but internal climate feedbacks modulating atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) are necessary to explain the full magnitude of glacial–interglacial climate variability. Identifying such feedbacks and linking them to orbitally paced forcing remains a challenge, impeding a comprehensive understanding of the glacial cycles. Orbital variations, determining the latitudinal distribution and seasonality of insolation, are primarily important for allowing the buildup of large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets. Meanwhile, the processes canonically understood to drive CO 2 drawdown and mediate ocean–atmosphere carbon partitioning are largely hosted in the far-flung Southern Ocean. This study explores the role of remote Northern Hemisphere temperature forcing in influencing Southern Ocean conditions that impact global ocean circulation and carbon content. In a set of idealized ocean–sea ice model simulations, we find that cooling air temperatures to glacial-like levels at the high northern latitudes (emulating the thermal effect of a large Northern Hemisphere ice sheet) drives a substantial CO 2 drawdown of 32 ppm—or 74% the magnitude of a simulation forced by globally glacial-like temperatures everywhere (43 ppm). Northern cooling is found to cool not only northern-sourced middepth waters but ultimately also global deep waters, resulting in a strong solubility-driven CO 2 drawdown component. It also drives several characteristic features of glacial periods, including expanded southern sea ice and a colder, saltier, and better stratified deep ocean, which contributes to air–sea CO 2 disequilibrium. These results demonstrate an interhemispheric connection between Northern Hemisphere conditions paced by orbital variations and Southern Hemisphere processes that modulate deep-ocean carbon content. Significance Statement Linking the orbital pacing of the ice ages—primarily expressed by the growth and decay of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets—to processes hosted in the Southern Ocean that can regulate ocean carbon storage has long posed a challenge. Here, we demonstrate using idealized simulations a clear influence of Northern Hemisphere cooling on Southern Ocean conditions and global ocean circulation and carbon content, which in turn draws down carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from the atmosphere. This result underscores the importance of conditions in the high northern latitudes in shaping the ocean–atmosphere carbon balance, offering lessons about the interconnectedness of remote regions that are relevant to both past and contemporary climate change.

title: Ocean carbon sequestration during glacial climates due to combined Antarctic sea ice expansion and ocean circulation change
abstract: Glacial-interglacial transitions punctuate Earth’s Quaternary climate, accompanied by substantial atmospheric carbon dioxide and ocean carbon storage changes. The cause of atmospheric carbon drawdown during glaciations is uncertain, involving many mechanisms whose interactions are poorly understood. Here, we show that the combined expansion of Antarctic sea ice and associated changes in the meridional overturning efficiently sequester carbon in the ocean abyss, leading to a decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide. In contrast, changes in sea ice and circulation individually result in ocean carbon dioxide outgassing. When sea ice expansion and circulation changes act together, they enhance biological carbon storage by reducing ocean-atmosphere fluxes in the Southern Ocean, without invoking external drivers of the biological pump. This reduction inhibits the outgassing of upwelled remineralized carbon and promotes its resubduction into the abyss. Together, these results reveal a reinforcing feedback linking atmospheric cooling, Antarctic sea ice expansion, and ocean circulation changes to enhanced biological carbon storage and atmospheric carbon dioxide drawdown.

title: Bistability of ice-shelf cavity circulation and melt under coastal polynya forcing
abstract: arXiv:2610.35359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Antarctic ice shelves play a key role in controlling the mass loss of the Antarctic Ice Sheet. Increasing evidence from regional studies suggests the possibility of abrupt transitions from low to high basal melt regimes under future climate forcing. The computational cost and complexity of these realistic simulations yet limit their ability to systematically investigate the steady-state response of ice shelves to incremental forcing, the reversibility of abrupt transitions and the underlying positive feedback loops. Here, we report a detailed analysis of abrupt regime changes in an ice-shelf cavity with idealized geometry, subject to prescribed temperature and salinity stratifications in the far field and near-ice-front surface salt fluxes representing the impact of sea-ice production in coastal polynyas. We show that a cold regime emerges when the buoyancy loss in the polynya is sufficient to trigger deep convection, while a warm regime develops otherwise. The steady response of the system exhibits hysteresis, characteristic of irreversible transitions, and scaling laws are proposed for both melt rates and transition thresholds. We demonstrate that bistability emerges when a gyre recirculates the meltwater within the ice-shelf front area. The bistable forcing range increases with far-field ocean temperature but decreases with background stratification. We also show that increasing horizontal viscosity limits bistability, which may explain the range of behaviors reported in previous studies.

title: Rate-induced tipping of ice sheets due to visco-elastic Earth response under idealized conditions
abstract: Here we examine the tipping dynamics of instability-prone marine ice sheets in interaction with the underlying solid Earth in a simplified model setup. The idealized ensemble simulations allow a systematic investigation of (1) bifurcation-induced and (2) rate-induced ice-sheet tipping for a wide range of representative Antarctic solid-Earth structures. We examine the conditions that lead to shifts in the tipping thresholds, the occurrence of rate-induced tipping or grounding-line overshoots.

title: The overshoot integral can inform climate science and policy beyond 1.5 °C of warming
abstract: Abstract The carbon budget framework has served as the dominant organising principle for climate science and policy, linking cumulative emissions to peak warming and providing a tractable scalar constraint for international negotiations. With 1.5 °C exceedance now imminent and virtually all mitigation scenarios involving substantial temperature overshoot before net-negative emissions could return temperatures to target, the budget framework’s utility for evaluating and minimising risk generated by warming risks becoming diminished. We propose a complementary organising principle: the overshoot integral, defined as the time-integrated temperature exceedance above a policy-relevant threshold, with units of °C·years. Analogous to degree-heating weeks in coral bleaching prediction and positive degree-days in glaciology, the overshoot integral captures both the magnitude and duration of exceedance in a single scalar quantity. Applying this metric to future climate pathways, we show that pathways with similar peak temperatures can differ by more than two orders of magnitude in their cumulative degree-year burden. Applied to CMIP7 ScenarioMIP/FaIR (Finite Amplitude Impulse Response simple climate model) trajectories, calculating overshoot integrals reveal substantial differences in cumulative thermal exposure across pathways. For Earth-system impacts whose response dynamics integrate forcing over time, spanning marine habitat, permafrost carbon and mountain glaciers, we show that cumulative thermal exposure captured by the overshoot integral contains impact-relevant information not captured by peak warming alone. A simple risk formulation combining peak and cumulative exposure improves out-of-sample prediction across all three systems. That the overshoot integral is best understood not as a reversible account that can be debited and credited, but as a cumulative dose should inform climate policy and science in the increasingly warmer future.

title: The uncertain impacts of an 1.5 °C overshoot-and-decline scenario on carbon stocks and productivity in terrestrial ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Overshoot scenarios, in which global temperatures peak and then decline through emission reductions and CO 2 removal, are increasingly central to climate policy as we are already approaching 1.5 °C warming. Yet the ecological reversibility of such pathways remains poorly understood, even though the trajectories of productivity and carbon stocks in terrestrial ecosystems have major implications for land-based carbon sink projections. Here we draw on four complementary lines of research to study the land carbon sink under overshoot: (i) CMIP6 models project declines in net ecosystem productivity (NEP) after peak warming. Nevertheless, NEP remains positive, leading to a stabilisation of the carbon stocks in terrestrial vegetation (cVeg). The CO 2 ramp up-down model experiment by CDRMIP underscores that these models predict near-reversibility of the vegetation carbon stock. (ii) A systematic review on global change experiments identified 256 papers (warming, drought, irrigation or elevated CO 2 , all elements of an overshoot scenario). However, only 15 included a recovery phase following treatment. This reveals a gap in experimental design for understanding ecosystem responses under overshoot conditions. Where recovery was assessed, responses were mixed, with persistent legacy effects documented after drought. (iii) Modern-day overshoot analogues, including two El Niño events and the 2018–2020 European droughts, show that compound heat and drought can cause carbon losses that recover slowly, with repeated extremes progressively reducing ecosystem resilience. (iv) Paleoclimate records from the Holocene Climatic Optimum and the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum demonstrate that exceeding ecological thresholds can trigger vegetation changes and carbon cycle feedbacks that long outlast the climatic perturbation itself. Together, these findings show that the trajectory of the terrestrial carbon sink during climate overshoot is uncertain, because ecosystem responses are often delayed, nonlinear, and threshold dependent.

Emplacement of an englacial lava-fed delta at Katla volcano, south Iceland: Timing, paleoenvironment and landscape modification
journal: Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research
abstract: Glaciovolcanic products are important proxies for paleoenvironmental reconstructions in volcanic regions, especially when these products can be dated. A lava-fed delta sequence exposed 400 to 800 m asl on the flanks of Katla volcano, south Iceland, erupted and was emplaced into a past englacial lake. A rising passage zone between subaqueous and subaerial lithofacies indicates a dynamic lake surface level during delta progradation with a final elevation ~790 m asl. The glacier surface surrounding the lake is estimated to have been ~900 m asl, and the glacier was smaller than the Younger Dryas maximum. Two 40 Ar/ 39 Ar ages for lavas in the delta sequence were determined: a basal lava (13.6 ± 3.6 ka) and an upper lava (11.1 ± 3.2 ka). These ages are supported by the stratigraphic position of the lava-fed delta above sediments containing pumice and obsidian clasts compositionally identical to the ~12 ka Vedde Ash. The age-constrained model for englacial emplacement of the lava-fed delta contributes to sparse empirical evidence for ice sheet thickness and extent in south Iceland at the end of the last glacial period. The lava ages also provide estimates of the incision rates of canyons that have dissected the lava-fed delta from the flank of Katla volcano. Formation of ~200 m-deep canyons since the emplacement of the upper lavas indicate rapid incision enhanced by episodic outburst flooding associated with subsequent eruptions and destabilisation of the glacier with climate amelioration. Thus, careful consideration of landscape modification is crucial when reconstructing the evolution of glaciovolcanic areas.

title: Climate‐modulated accumulation and erosion of sediments in the Rodderberg crater basin for the last 439 ka (East Eifel Volcanic Field, Germany)
abstract: ABSTRACT Glacial/interglacial climate cycles since marine isotope stage (MIS) 12 influenced the discontinuous and 73 m‐long sediment record from the volcanic crater of Rodderberg in the East Eifel Volcanic Field, Germany. High‐resolution grain size and geochemical data have been valued by numerical dating techniques (radiocarbon and luminescence dating, tephrochronology), providing an environmental reconstruction since the Middle Pleistocene (439 ka). The observed hydroclimatic variability, along with silting‐up of the crater basin, significantly influenced depositional processes. This results in the formation of laminated, sand‐rich, and organic‐rich sediments during interglacial periods, as well as layered, silt‐rich minerogenic loess derivatives during glacial periods. According to chronology, the crater basin desiccated during MIS 8 and MIS 5, causing erosion of the interglacials related to MIS 9 and MIS 5e. The combined evidence over five glacial/interglacial cycles suggests a depositional evolution from a deep crater lake during MIS 12–10, desiccation during MIS 8 with erosion of MIS 9, a shallow lake for MIS 7, and a desiccating wetland during MIS 6, followed by deposition of loess (MIS 6‐2) and a Holocene soil (MIS 1).

title: Pangu-Weather underestimates the 2019 European summer heatwave: A storyline comparison with ICON
abstract: Abstract Although it has been demonstrated that data-driven models can outperform physical models in simulating mean states, their capabilities to simulate extremes and their generalizability across climate scenarios remain questionable. This study compares Pangu-Weather to the physics-based ICON-CLM model in simulating peak of the July 2019 European summer heatwave and its unfolding in +2, +3, and +4 K future warmer scenarios, following a storyline approach. We initialize both Pangu-Weather and ICON-CLM using global storyline simulations from the coupled climate model AWI-CM1, which were spectrally nudged towards ERA5 reanalysis to maintain the large-scale flow and to accurately assess the impacts on heatwave severity due to thermodynamic changes only. To quantify uncertainties in Pangu-Weather’s predictions, the random field perturbation (RFP) technique is used to generate probabilistic forecasts. The study reveals that Pangu-Weather shows a systematic cold bias of about 2 – 3° C over the heatwave core region in both present and future warmer scenarios. Pangu-Weather fails to capture maximum 2-m temperature (T 2 m ) exceeding 45° C in +3 and over a limited area in +4 K global warming scenarios compared to ICON-CLM, indicating its limitations to accurately predict out-of-sample extremes even in an ensemble framework. Further, the maximum T 2 m response is linearly dependent on global warming levels consistent with ICON-CLM simulations but with reduced warming amplification. Additionally, it shows that Pangu-Weather needs enough time to leave the trajectory specified by forcing data. Our study emphasizes that the storyline approach and comparison with physics-based models show a promising way to test data-driven models for their applicability to warmer climate conditions.

title: Bayesian Synchronization of Proxy Paleorecords with Reference Chronologies
abstract: ABSTRACT Many scientific fields compare two or more noisy time series that integrate the same process but are recorded on different time scales. In paleoclimate studies, for example, proxy measurements are collected versus stratigraphic depth in a climate archive and then converted to calendar time. Synchronizing two proxy records often requires estimating an alignment that maps the depth (or preliminary age) of an input record onto the calendar‐time scale of an absolutely‐dated target record so that corresponding proxy signals line up. Existing alignment approaches are generally optimization‐based and return a single transformation, providing limited formal uncertainty quantification. Here, we introduce BSync, a Bayesian synchronization framework that treats alignments as inference over a monotone time‐mapping function to match an input to a target record. The alignment is expressed as a transformation of the input depth (or age) scale to match the target record, achieved through a link function that locally expands and compresses the input scale. The model is parameterized through interpretable local rate parameters, enabling the specification of priors on deposition times to regularize the alignment toward physically plausible deformations. BSync jointly infers the aligned chronology and provides posterior uncertainty for the time‐warping function and the resulting age scale. In synthetic data experiments and a real‐data case study, BSync yields well‐calibrated credible intervals for the aligned time scale and achieves more accurate alignments than a state‐of‐the‐art automated method, particularly when independent age constraints are sparse.

title: Reduced Evapotranspiration Decreases Land Precipitation Despite Enhanced Moisture Convergence: Insights from Perturbed Parameter Ensembles of Earth System Models
abstract: Abstract Both canonical theory and climate model simulations predict an increase in globally averaged precipitation with radiatively-forced warming. However, terrestrial processes control surface water and energy fluxes, and therefore can impact surface temperatures independently of radiative forcing. Here, we investigate the sensitivity of the global hydrological cycle to warming induced by changes in land surface conditions using perturbed parameter ensembles from two climate models, which sample a broad range of evapotranspiration (ET) states through modifications to land model parameters. The parameters are perturbed within the range of observationally constrained uncertainty and alter ET through different land surface pathways. We find that reduced ET drives warming yet decreases land-mean precipitation, which we link to strong decreases in near-surface relative humidity from warming. These decreases in relative humidity overcome increases in specific humidity and moisture convergence over land, which are also caused by shifts in large-scale circulation. We explain the tropical precipitation response to ET forcing with a simple scaling that relates changes in the land-ocean contrast in relative humidity to land-mean precipitation change. Further, the suppressed ET induces a shortwave cloud response that amplifies warming. Our results highlight that changes to land surface properties at the magnitude of parametric uncertainty influence warming and precipitation. ET-driven warming reduces land precipitation, opposite in sign to the precipitation increase from radiatively-forced warming. This response is not directly captured by scalings of the global hydrological cycle with radiative forcing. We therefore establish the potential significance of terrestrial ecosystem functioning, and its response to climate change, for hydroclimate.

title: Near-Future Strengthening of ENSO-Related Sea Ice Variability in We st Antarctica
abstract: Abstract The increasing interannual variability of Antarctic sea ice near West Antarctica underscores the need to understand how El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnections may shape future sea ice changes. Using simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6, this study investigates the projected impacts of near-future ENSO variability on Antarctic sea ice. ENSO teleconnections are found to primarily influence Antarctic sea ice from austral winter through spring, and this influence is projected to strengthen in the near future. We show that the strengthened teleconnection is driven mainly by enhanced tropical forcing with the structural changes in tropical sea surface temperatures and precipitation, with a smaller contribution from changes in the midlatitude jet waveguide. These mechanisms are further supported by idealized nudging experiment using a dry dynamic core model. The strengthened teleconnection deepens the ENSO-induced mid-tropospheric circulation anomaly near West Antarctica, enhancing warm-air advection and the resulting sea ice anomalies. Overall, these changes are projected to increase Antarctic sea ice variability in the near future, highlighting the importance of understanding how evolving ENSO teleconnections may modulate Antarctic climate variability.

title: Global-scale variability of glacier velocity and mass loss across terminus environments
abstract: Abstract The environment in which a glacier terminates can strongly influence its behaviour, stability and future evolution, yet the relationship between terminus type and glacier dynamics at the global scale remains poorly constrained. Here we present a globally-complete classification of glacier termini distinguishing between land, lake, marine and shelf environments, and integrate it with datasets of glacier geometry, dynamics and climate. We show that although lake-, marine- and shelf-terminating glaciers comprise only 3.2% of glaciers globally, they account for over half of global glacier area and mass loss. We also show that lake- and marine-terminating glaciers flow, on average, 10% and 44% faster than land-terminating glaciers, respectively. Furthermore, specific (area-normalised) mass loss rates at lake-terminating glaciers are 57% greater than those at land- and marine-terminating glaciers. Our findings underscore the need for improved representation of non-land glacier termini in models of glacier evolution and sea-level rise, and suggest that distinguishing the environmental and geometric controls of termini on glacier dynamics remains an important challenge for future research.

title: Historical geomorphology and structural glaciology of south-western Admiralty Bay, King George Island, Antarctica
abstract: This study presents a 1:8000 geomorphological and structural glaciological map of south-western Admiralty Bay, King George Island, based on a 1979 aerial survey. The map covers an area of 37.9 km2 and documents 16 462 structures and landforms. Large-scale landscape characteristics are determined by bedrock geology sculpted by overlying ice masses. The glaciers can be broadly separated into highly-crevassed tidewater glaciers, and less dynamic land-terminating glaciers. Proglacial areas contain ice-cored terrain abandoned by receding ice masses, with paraglacial and periglacial features superimposed on larger-scale landforms. Between 1979 and 2025, glacier cover decreased by 7.6 km2 or 25.5%, with the recession of tidewater glaciers exposing 5.8 km of new coastline and increasing marine surface area by 0.9 km2. This map provides a historical foundation for glaciological and landscape evolution studies, in addition to investigations that monitor changing terrestrial and marine ecosystems in a warming climate.

title: Climate Change and the Stability of Glacier-Fed River Systems: Implications for Water Security in Vulnerable Regions
journal: Journal of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination
abstract: This study examines how climate change is reshaping the stability of glacier fed river systems and the implications for water security in vulnerable regions. Glaciers function as natural water storage, moderating seasonal and interannual variability, yet rising temperatures and altered precipitation regimes are accelerating glacier retreat worldwide. Using an integrated methodological framework combining climate data, glacier mass balance modelling, hydrological simulation, and water security indicators, the study assesses observed and projected changes in river flow magnitude, timing, variability, and extremes across glacier dependent basins. Results show widespread and persistent glacier mass loss, with short term increases in meltwater runoff followed by long term declines in river discharge as ice reserves diminish. Seasonal peak flows are shifting earlier in the year, while late season low flows are becoming more pronounced, reducing flow reliability during periods of high demand. Increased interannual variability and more frequent hydrological extremes further undermine river system stability. These changes translate directly into declining water availability, reduced predictability, and heightened risk for agriculture, hydropower generation, domestic supply, and aquatic ecosystems. The discussion highlights strong spatial differences driven by climatic setting, glacier characteristics, and governance capacity, demonstrating that vulnerability is unevenly distributed across regions. The findings underscore the limitations of water management frameworks based on historical conditions and emphasize the need for adaptive and forward-looking strategies. By explicitly linking cryospheric change to river stability and water security, this study informs climate hydrology research and supports policy planning adaptation.

title: Miocene−Pliocene Nenana Gravel deposition in response to tectonic denudation of the Alaska Range (USA)
abstract: Disentangling the effects of tectonics and Pliocene−Pleistocene climate forcing on rates of erosion remains key to understanding hypothesized feedbacks among these processes. In central Alaska (United States), deposition of the Nenana Gravel has long been attributed to foreland basin sedimentation coupled to tectonically controlled Miocene−Pliocene Alaska Range exhumation. However, recent cosmogenic burial dating of the lower Nenana Gravel implies that deposition did not begin until ca. 2.3 Ma, consistent with Alaska Range erosion driven by concurrent intensified glaciation during Pleistocene global climate changes. Our new 3.67 ± 0.75 Ma cosmogenic 26Al/10Be isochron burial age at the top of the Nenana Gravel exposed at the Suntrana section indicates that deposition concluded ∼1 m.y. before the previously reported onset. We show that the prior data do not support early Pleistocene burial, but instead yield a 5.5 ± 1.5 Ma simple 26Al/10Be burial age of initial Nenana Gravel deposition, consistent with tephrochronologically constrained 6.7 ± 0.1 Ma strata that conformably underlie the gravel. Deposition of the ∼800-m-thick Nenana Gravel exposed at the Suntrana section thus started between 6.7 ± 0.1 Ma and 5.5 ± 1.5 Ma and concluded by 3.67 ± 0.75 Ma, concurrent with increased Alaska Range exhumation rates associated with tectonic forcing at ca. 7−6 Ma. The Nenana Gravel therefore records Alaska Range denudation induced by Miocene−Pliocene tectonics, and not early Pleistocene climate.

title: EnsAI: an emulator for atmospheric ammonia ensembles
abstract: EnsAI is a newly developed artificial intelligence based program for efficiently generating ensembles of atmospheric surface ammonia concentrations that can be used in emissions inversions systems. Ensemble-based data assimilation methods are widely used for assimilation and emissions inversions, but are usually very computationally demanding. Once trained, EnsAI can run thousands of times faster than the physics-based models when run on graphics processing units.

title: A conceptual model of seasonal groundwater storage and meltwater transfer through a frontal moraine in the Chilean semiarid Andes (30°S)
abstract: The hydrology of (semi)arid Andean regions is strongly controlled by the cryosphere, particularly debris-free glaciers and snowmelt. Glacial systems are commonly connected to proglacial landforms, an interaction that determines the fate of meltwater by storing and transferring it to the wider catchment. This study investigates the hydrological role of a frontal moraine in regulating water delivery from the glacial system to the proglacial stream and the downstream environment. We combined surface-based geophysics, multi-temporal remote sensing and hydrological monitoring to characterise the internal structure and seasonal surface water dynamics of a moraine in the frontal area of the Tapado glacier complex, Chilean semiarid Andes. Geophysical observations suggest that the investigated area of the moraine is not dominated by glacial ice but instead consists predominantly of detrital material with high near-surface water content and deep high-resistivity zones consistent with limited seasonal interstitial ice mixed with unfrozen water. Surface water analyses on and in the immediate surroundings of the moraine showed that surface water is highly seasonal. Surface water observations indicate that pond growth during the early ablation season is consistent with limited infiltration due to seasonal interstitial ice at depth, whereas progressive pond drainage and changes in the proglacial stream signal suggest increasingly efficient subsurface water connectivity and water-transfer later in the season. Together, these observations support a conceptual model in which the moraine temporarily stores groundwater during the early ablation season and progressively increases subsurface connectivity as seasonal interstitial ice degrades, thereby regulating the timing of meltwater transfer toward the proglacial spring and stream. Our results highlight the importance of proglacial moraines as active groundwater storage and transfer components in deglaciating catchments and emphasize the need for targeted hydrological characterisation and monitoring from these landforms to better constrain current and future water availability in cryosphere-dependent mountain regions.

title: Differentiating Westerly and Asian monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean since the late Pliocene
abstract: Asian dust flux is a fundamental regulator of global climate and marine biogeochemical cycles, yet it is difficult to separate the dust fractions delivered to the tropical Pacific Ocean by the Westerlies and East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM). We present a 4-million-year record of eolian evolution from the Philippine Sea to deconvolve these two distinct transport systems on the basis of grain-size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting. Our results show that the Westerlies component is primarily derived from hyper-arid deserts, whereas the EAWM-driven component originates from the semi-arid margins of East and Central Asia. Of importance is the finding that Westerly-driven transport reflects a coherent response to global cooling and hemispheric thermal gradients, whilst the Asia monsoon contribution is mediated by vegetation cover. We further demonstrate that hydroclimatic fluctuations in EAWM marginal zones modulate dust availability through vegetation-induced surface roughness and pedogenic refinement, resulting in a pronounced non-linear relationship between dust flux and wind energetics. This suggests the ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus the tropical ocean, necessitating integration of dynamic vegetation impacts and anthropogenic landscape interventions on dust into Earth System Models to predict global carbon cycling in a warming world. “Ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus on the tropical ocean, shown using grain size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting of a 4-million-year-long sediment record from the Philippine Sea”

title: State-resolved multimodal contributions to stratospheric polar vortex predictability
abstract: arXiv:2605.13417v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dynamical basis of stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) predictability remains unclear, particularly the relative roles of persistence, structural variability, and cross-level coupling. Here we combine eigen microstate theory with mesoscopic Granger-causality analysis of ERA5 geopotential height fields to quantify the predictive contributions of eigen microstates. We show that short-term predictability is dominated by the persistence of the leading stratospheric state, whereas higher-order stratospheric structures and tropospheric variability provide additional predictive information at subseasonal leads. Including these additional states increases the all-winter 30-day prediction correlation from 0.24 to 0.33 and reduces forecast error. These contributions exhibit strong lead-time dependence and vary between winters with and without sudden stratospheric warmings. Part of this predictive information overlaps with that contained in preceding 100 hPa eddy heat flux, linking state-resolved predictability to wave-related circulation variability. Our results unify SPV predictability within a multimodal, state-resolved framework and provide a physically interpretable pathway.

title: Early to Mid‐Holocene molluscan community dynamics in Billefjorden, central Svalbard: the interplay of local geomorphology and regional climate
abstract: The postglacial evolution of High Arctic coastal environments is recorded in the rich fossiliferous archives of raised marine terraces. This study employs a multi‐proxy approach combining molluscan community analysis, taphonomy and sedimentology to reconstruct the Early to Mid‐Holocene environmental dynamics of the Mimerdalen embayment in the Billefjorden area of central Svalbard. Our results indicate that local benthic succession was driven by a complex interplay of glacio‐isostatic rebound and fluctuating sediment supply rather than simple climatic warming. We identify a four‐stage evolutionary trajectory: (1) an initial glaciomarine, brackish‐water phase dominated by the pioneer taxa Mya truncata and Hiatella arctica ; (2) a transition to fully marine conditions that facilitated the expansion of thermophilous species ( Mytilus edulis and Arctica islandica ); (3) a return to restricted brackish conditions due to forced regression and basin shallowing; and (4) a transition towards modern open‐fjord equilibrium, as slower glacio‐isostatic uplift and Mid‐Holocene Neoglacial cooling led to the disappearance of the thermally demanding taxa. Although not directly radiocarbon dated, valves of Arctica islandica and Zirfaea crispata are stratigraphically associated with dated M. truncata , suggesting their presence as early as ~10.4 cal. ka BP. This potentially advances their known regional arrival by up to 600 and 300 years, respectively, with A. islandica persisting until ~7.7 cal. ka BP. Comparisons with the Kapp Ekholm reference section demonstrate that local geomorphological stability and ephemeral disturbances, such as hyperpycnal deltaic input, were critical drivers of biodiversity, enabling the establishment of thermally demanding species. Ultimately, our findings confirm that Early Holocene sea temperatures significantly exceeded modern values, while emphasizing the overwhelming importance of salinity and seabed stability in shaping molluscan ecological structure. This study underscores the crucial role of local environmental heterogeneity in modulating the biological response to regional Holocene climate forcing in the High Arctic.

title: 4D sensitivity kernels for infrasound atmospheric propagation: considering the need and impact of time dependent observation operators for acoustic wave observations in data assimilation methods
abstract: arXiv:2610.36810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The long range propagation of acoustic waves in Earth's atmosphere is sensitive to winds and temperature variations in the upper atmosphere. Thus, infrasound observations have a strong potential to improve numerical weather models by data assimilation methods. However, because acoustic waves propagate slowly, the atmospheric parameters can change during the propagation of the acoustic waves. This change of atmosphere properties is usually not taken into account by infrasound simulation tools which generally assume stationary atmosphere models. In order to close this modeling gap, we present here a method to compute the linear sensitivities of infrasound observables to atmospheric parameters varying both in space and time. We show that adjoint based methods can easily handle this computation of 4D sensitivity kernels, also called time variable observation operators in the data assimilation community. Then, we discuss the capabilities of various data assimilation methods to handle such observation operators. We demonstrate that only variational methods with data assimilation windows longer than the propagation duration of the long range infrasound can accommodate these observations, as well as their ensemble counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of assimilating such long range infrasound observations, and we quantify the relative impact of linear approximation of observation operators and stationary approximation of the atmosphere model by assimilating propagation time observations of circumnavigating Lamb waves in Lorenz'96 low-order model. The results of this data assimilation experiment demonstrate that the time variability of atmospheric parameters should be taken into account even for infrasound propagation times limited to 2 or 3 time steps of the atmosphere model.

abstract: Abstract The boreal summer Asian–Australian monsoon (BSAAM) comprises several regional subsystems traditionally studied in isolation. This study provides a holistic perspective on the BSAAM and its modulation by pan-tropical sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTAs). The first mode (BSAAM1) captures Western Pacific Subtropical High anomalies and enhanced rainfall over India and the Yangtze–Huaihe River Basin. The second mode (BSAAM2) reflects Australian High variations, linked to increased rainfall over South China and the northern Bay of Bengal coast. BSAAM1 is associated with a tripole SSTA pattern spanning the Indian Ocean-Western Pacific, central–eastern Pacific, and tropical Atlantic (IOWP–CEP–TA tripole), while BSAAM2 corresponds to another tripole across the western Indian Ocean, Maritime Continent, and tropical CEP (WIO–MC–TCEP tripole). Both tripoles modulate their respective BSAAM modes through remote SST effects and local air-sea coupling. The seasonal evolution of these tripoles also differs markedly. BSAAM1 is governed by persistent SSTAs in the IOWP and TA, with rapid CEP cooling driven by thermodynamic wind-evaporation effects associated with Victoria Mode and dynamic zonal advection. BSAAM2 is driven by SSTA persistence in the MC, coupled with rapid warming in the WIO and TCEP, induced by thermodynamic wind-evaporation effects and dynamic zonal advection, respectively. Leveraging these physical insights, physically based empirical models are developed that outperform dynamical models in predicting the BSAAM, with forecast lead times extended to the preceding winter. This study presents a comprehensive understanding of how pan-tropical SSTAs modulate the BSAAM interannual variability and improve BSAAM seasonal predictability.

title: Geochemical and granulometric fingerprints of 8200 years of westerly wind variability in inner‐fjord lake sediments from Svalbard
abstract: The Arctic is warming faster than any other region on Earth. As sea ice diminishes, the surface boundary conditions, such as roughness and air–sea coupling, change and open‐water fetch increases. This may enhance wind forcing on Arctic coasts. Lake sediments can record these changes through the deposition of wind‐blown grains and elements, offering insights into past wind and climate dynamics. We reconstruct c . 8200 years of wind and climate variability using laminated sediments from a closed‐basin lake in central Spitsbergen, Svalbard archipelago, High Arctic. By integrating geochemical, visual and granulometric fingerprints within a multiproxy geostatistical framework, we link aeolian minerogenic input to specific catchment sources. Our findings show that iron (Fe)‐rich coarse silt‐sized clasts originate from distinct dolerite outcrops west and northwest of the lake, upwind of the dominant summer westerlies. This reveals a locally filtered westerly input that aligns with valley‐fjord channelling. We identify four phases of enhanced aeolian activity during the Mid‐ and Late Holocene, which occurred when local boundary conditions were favourable for entraining and transporting sediment into the basin. Major shifts in sediment sources and depositional conditions coincide with the end of the Holocene Thermal Maximum and the gradual onset of the Neoglacial. However, the reconstructed wind signal demonstrates a comparatively stable long‐term behaviour, with no clear correspondence to regional palaeoclimate records.

title: Contrasting Tropical SST Warming in Two Climate Models: The Roles of Winds, Clouds, Evaporative Cooling, and Ocean Dynamics
abstract: Abstract To investigate why climate models simulate diverse tropical Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) changes under greenhouse-gas forcing, we utilize two configurations of the Community Earth System Model (CESM2) that differ in their atmospheric component (CAM6 and CAM4). Under abrupt CO 2 quadrupling, CAM6 simulates over double the weakening of the east-west equatorial SST gradient compared to CAM4 by end-of-century. To understand this contrast, we conduct overriding experiments that replace wind stress, or wind stress and shortwave fluxes, with values from the preindustrial control experiment. In CAM6, low clouds amplify climate warming and act as a forcing and positive feedback on reductions in the east-west SST gradient. In contrast, in CAM4, low clouds act as a negative climate feedback and provide little contribution to the SST gradient reduction. In both models, interactive wind stress leads to a strong positive feedback (i.e., the Bjerknes feedback). The two models also diverge in their short-term SST responses: CAM6 exhibits an immediate weakening of the zonal SST gradient, while CAM4 initially shows a steepening. Our findings highlight the importance of shortwave radiative and Bjerknes feedbacks, evaporative cooling, and ocean dynamics, all of which control tropical Pacific SST pattern formation.

title: 40-kyr of environmental history of the southeastern sector of paleolake Cuitzeo, central-western Mexico: Insights from abiotic and biotic proxies
abstract: We present a multiproxy reconstruction of environmental changes recorded in the southeastern sector of Lake Cuitzeo (central-western Mexico) over the last ∼40 kyr. Our study integrates abiotic (major-element geochemistry, rock-magnetic parameters, pH, and electrical conductivity) and biotic proxies (diatoms and pollen) from a ∼10 m-long sedimentary core (Cz-07). This multiproxy approach provides a robust framework for identifying variations in terrigenous input, redox conditions, nutrient availability, carbonate precipitation, and hydrological balance, as well as the response of local vegetation to climate fluctuations. Comparing the Cz-07 record with previous data from a depocenter core reveals some spatial differences in the lake’s sensitivity to environmental changes. The sequence indicates generally low lake levels between ∼42 and ∼26.5 kyr BP, followed by pronounced environmental variability during the Last Glacial Maximum, including a marked dry episode at its onset. Enhanced runoff and predominantly oxic conditions characterize the interval from ∼17.5 to ∼11 kyr BP, encompassing the Bølling–Allerød and Younger Dryas events. During the early-to-middle Holocene (∼11.7–5 kyr BP), a progressive shift toward arid conditions is evidenced by increased carbonate precipitation, higher salinity, and reduced runoff. The most severe drought occurred during the middle Holocene, causing a substantial contraction of the lake’s southeastern sector. This arid phase aligns with middle Holocene drying trends reported in other lacustrine records across central Mexico.

title: Diversity of South China Sea Marine Heatwave Intensity Trends
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the seasonal characteristics and physical drivers of marine heatwave (MHW) intensity trends in the South China Sea (SCS) during 1993–2022. Results reveal a robust, seasonally consistent north-south divergent pattern: MHW intensity has intensified pronouncedly in the northern and northwestern SCS while declining on decadal timescales in the southwestern basin, forming a "rich-get-richer, poor-get-poorer" contrast. Mixed-layer heat budget diagnostics show that enhanced net surface heat flux (Qnet), driven by increased shortwave radiation (SSR) and reduced latent heat loss, primarily causes MHW intensification in the northern and northwestern SCS. In contrast, changes in the South China Sea West Boundary Current (SCS WBC) dominate in the southwestern SCS, where a weakening northward WBC in summer and strengthening southward WBC in winter shift horizontal advection toward net cooling, and thereby weakens MHWs. Teleconnection analyses link this regional disparity to different large-scale climate modes across seasons. Strengthening of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) respectively increase SSR over the northern SCS during summer and winter, while the negative phase shift of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) and ENSO weakens anticyclonic forcing that modulates the SCS WBC in the southwestern SCS in both seasons. These findings highlight the importance of seasonal and regional heterogeneity in MHW dynamics for improving the prediction of extreme ocean warming in marginal seas.

title: Evolution of the Tibetan Plateau-Northern Indian Ocean thermal contrast since the last deglaciation and its regulation of the Indian Summer Monsoon
High- and low-latitude forcing on precipitation variations over the central Qilian Mountains since 18.5 ka
abstract: The moisture of the northeastern Tibetan Plateau is jointly shaped by the East Asian Summer Monsoon (EASM) and the mid-latitude Westerlies, the two key atmospheric circulation systems originating from low- and high-latitudes, respectively. Modern observations demonstrate that the intensity change and meridional position of the Westerlies directly modulate the EASM precipitation, which sustains vast human populations and ecosystems across East Asia. However, the interaction between these two systems over geological time remains controversial, partly due to controversies in the reconstructed past precipitation intensity. Here, we present a high-resolution multi-proxy loess record (ZES) spanning the past 18.5 ka from the central Qilian Mountains, located in the monsoon marginal zone where both systems jointly operate. We first found that loess–paleosol carbonate δ 18 O of ZES record captures a summer signal and covaries inversely with δ 13 C, which tracks monsoon precipitation intensity. Together with comparisons between modern observations and geological records, this constrains EASM-dominated precipitation. We then establish a robust EASM index from multiple independent proxies including magnetic susceptibility, total carbonate content, dolomite content, carbonate δ 13 C, and colour reflectance. Our results reveal that EASM precipitation responded to combined high- and low-latitude forcing on both millennial timescales during the Last Deglaciation and orbital timescales manifested in the long-term trend since 18.5 ka, with the pre-Boreal oscillation offering complementary insights into early-Holocene centennial-scale interactions. The EASM precipitation intensity was suppressed during the Last Deglaciation, strengthened gradually through the early Holocene, peaked from ∼7.5 to 1.8 ka, and subsequently declined. Direct comparison of Westerlies and EASM signals retrieved from the same loess sequence reveals coupled interaction between the two systems since the mid-late Holocene, with westerly intensification accompanying monsoon strengthening. These findings indicate bidirectional linkage between high- and low-latitude systems and further suggest that, under continued global warming, the monsoon marginal zone of northwestern China may experience a progressive increase in precipitation.

abstract: The southeastern Tibetan Plateau (SETP), a critical component of the “Asian Water Tower”, hosts a large concentration of maritime temperate glaciers that are highly sensitive to climate change. However, persistent cloud cover, seasonal snow, and supraglacial debris complicate consistent long-term glacier mapping, while the use of static glacier boundaries may introduce temporal mismatches in altimetry-based glacier mass-change estimates. In this study, we developed a multi-source data-fusion framework on Google Earth Engine (GEE) to reconstruct glacier-area changes in the SETP from 2000 to 2025 at five-year intervals and 30 m spatial resolution. Random Forest classifiers were used to integrate Landsat and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 synthetic-aperture-radar data, and NASADEM-derived topographic information, supporting glacier delineation under complex surface and atmospheric conditions. The reconstructed glacier area decreased from 8,083 ± 664 km2 in 2000 to 6,228 ± 572 km2 in 2025, corresponding to a cumulative loss of 22.9 ± 3.6% and a mean loss rate of 80.51 ± 10.51 km2 yr−1. The mean area-loss rates were 51.31 ± 6.51 km2 yr−1 during 2000–2010 and 92.99 ± 15.55 km2 yr−1 during 2010–2025, indicating a higher average loss rate in the later period. By combining satellite-altimetry-derived elevation changes from ICESat, CryoSat-2, and ICESat-2 with the reconstructed time-varying glacier areas, we estimated a mean glacier mass-change rate of −6.51 ± 1.22 Gt yr−1 during 2003–2022. Compared with using a fixed 2003 glacier area, the time-varying-area calculation reduced the estimated mass-loss magnitude by 0.63 Gt yr−1, equivalent to 8.8% of the fixed-area estimate. These results indicate that incorporating time-varying glacier areas can reduce temporal mismatch in altimetry-based mass-change estimation and improve the temporal consistency of regional glacier mass-change assessments.

title: Detecting Month-Dependent Predictability with Periodic Autoregressive Models: Reemergence and Predictability Barriers
abstract: Abstract The climate system displays a seasonal cycle not only in its mean state, but also in predictability and variance. In particular, month-dependent autocorrelation functions (ACFs) reveal seasonal variations in persistence and are used routinely to characterize such phenomena as the spring predictability barrier in El Niño forecasts and the wintertime reemergence of sea surface temperature anomalies. However, detection of such behavior in climate data has often relied on heuristic procedures tailored to specific applications that are difficult to generalize to other applications. This paper proposes a general approach to detecting month-dependent ACFs based on Periodic Autoregressive (PAR) models, which extend standard autoregressive models by allowing parameters to vary with month. Specifically, a likelihood ratio test is used to determine if a PAR provides a significantly better fit than a stationary model with month-invariant parameters. Externally forced variability is incorporated through additional forcing terms. The resulting model provides a self-consistent representation of both internal and forced variability. Applying the test to observational records of sea surface temperature reveals distinct regions with statistically significant month-dependence in their ACFs. These include the tropical Pacific, where the method identifies the canonical spring predictability barrier, and several midlatitude regions displaying the statistical signature of reemergence. The test also identifies a previously undocumented seasonal rebound in the ACF over the Guinea Dome region of the northeastern tropical Atlantic. It is further shown that the widely used Seasonal Autoregressive (SAR) model cannot capture in a parsimonious manner the spring predictability barrier or reemergence.

title: Probabilistic adjustment of seasonal forecasts using cVAE with a non-parametric decoder: A case study of Arctic sea ice predictions
abstract: arXiv:2605.29172v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Seasonal climate predictions support planning and risk management by offering early information of the likely climate conditions in the coming months, and associated uncertainties. Ensemble forecasts enable this by simulating many plausible outcomes, allowing predictions to be expressed as usable probabilities. Large ensembles and high-resolution forecasts strengthen this by better sampling uncertainty and capturing finer-scale processes but come with significant computational cost. Moreover, forecast ensembles drift and exhibit systematic biases and spatio-temporal errors that grow with lead time, requiring careful post-processing and calibration. A probabilistic post-processing framework based on conditional Variational Autoencoders (cVAEs) was developed at the Canadian Center for Climate Modeling and Analysis to generate large ensembles of adjusted seasonal predictions of Arctic sea ice. The generative model was designed to learn the observational distribution conditioned on the biased model prediction. This enables generation of arbitrarily large ensembles of calibrated, bias corrected forecasts with improved skill. Here, we extend this framework to a Generalized Variational Inference problem to address the loss of fine-scale energy and the characteristic blurriness, a known limitation of standard cVAEs. Specifically, we employ a generator in place of the Gaussian parametrized decoder in cVAE and use Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) in the objective function instead of the Gaussian log-likelihood. We further use a higher resolution target dataset compared to the raw forecast. We show that the adjusted forecasts are better calibrated, more consistent with the observational distribution, and exhibit smaller errors than benchmark predictions, while also enhancing the resolution of the raw forecasts and improving sharpness and spectral power relative to the standard cVAE.

title: FASST: A Compact Stateless Atmosphere Model for Long-Term Ocean Coupling
abstract: arXiv:2610.36297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupled climate simulations are computationally expensive, largely because of the atmosphere. We introduce FASST, a coupled climate model that retains the prognostic POP2 ocean while replacing the atmosphere and sea ice with lightweight U-Net emulators. The atmospheric emulator is diagnostic, predicting surface fluxes from the evolving ocean-ice state every $6$ simulated hours, while the sea-ice emulator advances the ice state monthly. For $140$ years of unforced integration, FASST maintains a stable global-mean climate without SST restoring, with post-transient global-mean SST of $291.30 \pm 0.22\mathrm{K}$ compared with $291.25 \pm 0.10\mathrm{K}$ in CESM$2$ piControl. FASST also captures interannual Ni\~no-$3.4$ variability, although with weaker amplitude than CESM ($0.62\mathrm{K}$ versus $1.02\mathrm{K}$). These results demonstrate that a stateless learned atmosphere can sustain stable, free-running coupled climate simulations over century-scale integrations.

title: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
abstract: If a nuclear war happened, firestorms induced by nuclear detonations in urban areas could inject black carbon (BC) into the upper atmosphere, disrupting global climate. title: Dynamical-Model-Informed Stochastic Flow Matching for Global Probabilistic Subseasonal Forecasting of Means and Extremes
abstract: arXiv:2610.30159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-based models provide skillful subseasonal forecasts but suffer from systematic biases, weakened teleconnections, and parameterized physics, while very large ensembles remain computationally expensive. Purely data-driven models also see too few realizations of the low-frequency modes that provide subseasonal predictability. We introduce methodname, a hybrid framework that converts modelshort subseasonal ensemble guidance into 90-member stochastic forecasts of weekly precipitation and 2 m temperature on a global 1-degree grid using a lead-aware flow-matching U-Net. Its stochastic prior initializes members with EOF perturbations conditioned on the Madden-Julian Oscillation, North Atlantic Oscillation, El Nino-Southern Oscillation, and lead week, allowing the learned flow to refine large-scale covariance rather than create it from white noise. On held-out 2021-2025 forecasts, empirical CRPS improves by 22.0% for precipitation and 25.6% for temperature in a same-initialization four-versus-four comparison, and by 32.2% and 34.0% in the 90-versus-four production comparison. Ablations across five training seeds show distinct gains from the structured prior and a learned error-variance pathway, with the prior contributing more. Verification over 120 observed-extreme cases shows positive CRPS skill, but the ensemble remains underdispersive, four-member upper quantiles are poorly resolved, and precipitation exceedance BSS is near neutral after week 1. Results support improved probabilistic skill and tail representation, but not calibrated operational rare-event probabilities. Case studies of the 2022 UK heatwave, 2023 California atmospheric rivers, and 2022 Pakistan floods illustrate the reach and limits of dynamically informed refinement.

title: Cleaner air strengthens the Pacific trade winds without a detectable change in El Nino
abstract: arXiv:2610.31236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Air quality policy will cut aerosol and ozone precursor emissions, and studies disagree on how the tropical Pacific circulation and the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) will respond. Here we show, in 12 Earth system models with and without air quality controls, that the cuts strengthen the Pacific trade winds and offset half to two thirds of the weakening projected without them. The response is absent with prescribed sea surface temperatures and detectable only after 2040. It is consistent with the Indian Ocean warming relative to the Pacific, which also ranks the responses to cuts made region by region. ENSO amplitude changes by less than a tenth of its value, the smallest change this ensemble could detect. The change implied by the mean state shift is a sixth of that, and an ENSO model trained without the reduced emission runs predicts none. El Nino's regional impacts still change, because the background climate does.

title: Integrating a global glacier model into local hydrological modeling: Impacts on melt contributions
abstract: Abstract. Snow and glacier meltwater are critical water resources for mountain regions, yet their accurate representation in hydrological models remains challenging. As climate change alters the timing and magnitude of melt contributions, accurate partitioning between snow and glacier sources becomes increasingly important. To address this challenge, this study couples the hydrological model HBV (as implemented in the Raven modeling framework) with the Global Glacier Evolution Model GloGEM and integrates a snow redistribution scheme for application across 14 glaciated headwater catchments in Switzerland. At this local catchment scale, we investigate whether glacier constraints and the addition of snow redistribution reduce parameter equifinality and increase the reliability of melt contribution estimates. Simulations are evaluated against observed streamflow, gridded snow water equivalent data, and glacier melt data based on observed mass balance. The gravitational snow redistribution algorithm successfully prevents unrealistic high-elevation snow accumulation and improves catchment average SWE simulation performance. Uncoupled HBV configurations outperform coupled HBV-GloGEM setups according to streamflow metrics. However, this superior performance is achieved by simulating glacier melt rates exceeding GloGEM estimates and glacier storage change data by factors of 2–3 in some catchments, effectively using glacier ice to offset precipitation biases in forcing data, which can be critical for climate change impact studies. Glacier melt contributions can vary by nearly an order of magnitude among best-performing parameter sets, highlighting severe parameter equifinality. Coupling with GloGEM, calibrated using glacier-specific geodetic mass balance, produces glacier melt consistent with observations and substantially improves identifiability of both glacier and snowmelt contributions. Despite lower streamflow performance metrics, glacier melt constraints prevent compensatory errors that would compromise projections as melt dynamics shift under climate change. Applying this framework to future climate scenarios and integrating additional constraints such as snow observations may further improve the reliability of melt contribution projections.

Covariance-Informed Ensemble Score Filtering: Embedding Localized Covariance Geometry into Score-Based Transport
abstract: arXiv:2610.32148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Background-error covariance models are central to atmospheric data assimilation because they spread partial observational information across space, variables, and dynamically coupled scales. Ensemble and variational methods exploit this covariance geometry efficiently, but their standard analysis formulations are largely built around Gaussian or locally quadratic approximations. Score-based ensemble filtering provides a framework for nonlinear distributional transport, but existing Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) formulations lack an intrinsic covariance-mediated pathway for propagating likelihood information from observed to unobserved state components. We introduce a covariance-informed ensemble score filter (CI-EnSF) that embeds localized forecast-error covariance geometry directly into the forward diffusion and reverse transport. The proposed forward diffusion is covariance-shaped in standardized state space and becomes isotropic under the corresponding control-variable transformation. This covariance structure continuously propagates observational information from observed to unobserved state components throughout the reverse transport analysis trajectory. Experiments with Lorenz-96 and surface quasi-geostrophic (SQG) dynamics show a clear regime dependence. For linear observations, a well-tuned LETKF is more accurate, while CI-EnSF maintains stable cycling and effective covariance-mediated information propagation. Under strongly nonlinear observations and under climatological initialization, CI-EnSF achieves lower analysis error and greater cycling robustness than Gaussian ensemble benchmarks such as the LETKF, with improvements extending across spatial scales in the nonlinear SQG experiment. These results suggest that the principal benefit of CI-EnSF arises from combining nonlinear distributional transport with the mature covariance geometry used in conventional data assimilation.

title: Impact of Cumulus Parameterization and Cloud Microphysics on WRF Simulation of an Extreme Rainfall Event over Maharashtra, India: A 3 by 3 Factorial Assessment
abstract: arXiv:2610.36944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating extreme monsoon rainfall over the Konkan coast and Western Ghats remains challenging at 9 km resolution, where convection is partly resolved and partly parameterised. This study evaluates the sensitivity of Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) simulations of the 5-7 July 2026 Maharashtra rainfall event to cumulus and cloud microphysics schemes. Nine simulations employed a 3 x 3 factorial design combining WSM6, WDM6 and Thompson microphysics with Kain-Fritsch, Tiedtke and Grell-Freitas cumulus schemes. Rainfall was evaluated against IMD 0.25-degree gridded observations, with IMERG and ERA5 as additional references. A descriptive factorial decomposition showed that cumulus parameterisation accounted for 97.3% of across-experiment variation in mean rainfall, 88.2% in RMSE and 84.7% in spatial correlation, while microphysics contributed 2.0%, 2.1% and 9.3%, respectively. Kain-Fritsch produced the highest spatial correlations (0.533-0.581) but substantially overestimated rainfall. Tiedtke achieved the smallest mean biases and RMSE, although compensating regional errors concealed a 28-34% rainfall deficit over the Konkan-Ghats belt and substantial underestimation on 7 July. Grell-Freitas showed large wet biases and relatively high RMSE. All nine simulations displaced the event-total rainfall maximum approximately 140-195 km northward. WSM6-Tiedtke achieved the lowest RMSE, whereas Thompson-Kain-Fritsch better represented the rainfall spatial pattern. The findings demonstrate that, for this event and fixed model configuration, cumulus parameterisation exerted substantially greater influence on simulated rainfall than cloud microphysics. However, a single-event, single-member experimental design does not establish a universally optimal physics configuration.

title: Hybrid ensemble forecasting combining physics-based and machine-learning predictions through spectral nudging
abstract: arXiv:2603.05570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the first application of spectral nudging in a probabilistic ensemble forecasting framework, combining the physics-based ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System ensemble (IFS-ENS) with forecasts from the probabilistic machine-learned AIFS-ENS ensemble. Large scales of virtual temperature and vorticity are relaxed toward the machine-learned forecasts, while mesoscale structures remain governed by the physics-based model. This hybrid ensemble shows substantial improvements in large-scale forecast skill, with gains in predictive skill extended by up to two days in the tropics and by approximately half a day in the extra-tropics relative to IFS-ENS. Despite nudging being applied only to upper-air fields, improvements are also found in several near-surface parameters. Tropical cyclone track forecasts improve significantly, consistent with improved representation of the large-scale steering flow, without degrading storm intensity or ensemble spread. These results demonstrate that spectral nudging can be successfully extended to ensemble prediction and provide an attractive pathway for combining machine-learned and physics-based weather prediction systems.

title: Climate change impacts on the predicted performance of optimized building-integrated photovoltaics
abstract: by Elyas Hannoufa, Eric Johlin Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) are a promising strategy for enhancing building energy performance and reducing carbon emissions. However, most design optimization studies rely on historical climate datasets that may fail to capture the operating conditions buildings will experience under climate change. This study develops a computational framework for the multi-objective optimization of BIPV envelope systems using future climate projections from the CanESM5 model under the SSP3-7.0 scenario. We analyze two system configurations, awning shades and thin-film window coatings, across four cities with diverse climates (Berlin, Los Angeles, Chicago, Singapore), comparing results from conventional EPW files, NASA 2023 historical data, and 2046–2050 climate scenarios. Optimization integrates electricity generation, thermal loads, and daylighting quality to capture building-level trade-offs. Results show that traditional EPW datasets systematically under-predict BIPV performance, particularly in Berlin and Los Angeles. Under 2046–2050 projected conditions, all four cities exhibit performance gains: substantial in Berlin, Chicago and Los Angeles, and marginal in Singapore, with the largest absolute gains in Los Angeles. By 2050, unshaded windows transition to consistently detrimental for building energy balance. Thin-film coatings achieve optimal outcomes at high absorptance, in the 80–90% range, contrary to current low-absorption design practice. Within the CanESM5 SSP3-7.0 scenario examined, these findings show that projected climate conditions can substantially reshape the modeled performance landscape of BIPV systems, emphasizing the need for forward-looking climate projections in building design optimization and the growing importance of BIPV for climate-adaptive and resilient urban buildings.

abstract: BorFIT is a novel training dataset for light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point cloud segmentation and tree species detection in boreal forests. Comprising 384 plots across Siberia, Canada, and Alaska, it features 16 530 manually segmented trees of 12 species. BorFIT supports artificial intelligence (AI) applications for analyzing species distribution, stand structure, and boreal forest response to climate change.

title: Linking rain-on-snow events to river floods in the Tianshan Mountains
abstract: Rain-on-snow (ROS) events are widely recognized as an important cryosphere–hydrology coupling mechanism, yet when and where ROS events translate into river floods remains poorly constrained, particularly in arid high-mountain regions. Here, we provide the first basin-scale assessment of potential flood-inducing ROS (ROS-PF) and actual river-flood-generating ROS (ROS-AF) events across the Tianshan Mountains. Using ERA5-Land reanalysis (1951–2019) and an observation-based reconstructed daily streamflow dataset covering 40 Tianshan watersheds, we link ROS forcing to reconstructed high-flow responses. ROS-PF events—defined by rainfall ≥10 mm occurring on snowpack with snow water equivalent ≥10 mm—are concentrated in spring (April–June) and mid-elevations (2.0–3.5 km), within a narrow temperature window of–0.24 ± 1.49 °C. Their frequency has increased significantly over the past seven decades, driven primarily by rising heavy rainfall occurrence rather than snow availability. On average, ROS-PF events contributed on average 14.7% of the 6-day snowmelt total and 8.3% of the 6-day available-water total across the Tianshan basins. Crucially, only ∼44% of ROS-PF events evolve into ROS-AF events, revealing strong basin-dependent conversion efficiency. Some basins like Pochengzi basin convert nearly all ROS-PF events into floods, while others exhibit high ROS-PF frequency but minimal flood response. Most ROS-AF events occur with a lag of up to six days, underscoring the importance of delayed hydrological responses. These findings demonstrate that ROS does not uniformly amplify flood risk but instead reorganizes flood-generation pathways under warming, with implications for flood forecasting and water management in arid mountain systems.

title: Forecasting carbon-risk hotspots ahead of the extreme 2026 El Ni\~no
abstract: arXiv:2610.16714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A potentially super El Ni\~no is forecasted in 2026, raising the need to anticipate land carbon-cycle risks before its impacts unfold. We develop a prospective early-warning framework that uses dynamic global vegetation models driven by an ensemble of ECMWF seasonal climate forecasts and machine-learning burned area predictions. Forecasts indicate a $0.23 \pm 0.21$ PgC reduction in global net biome productivity in the second half of 2026, with hotspots of sink weakening in eastern South America and elevated fire risk in Southeast Asia.
